name: Gillagréine

attributes.attribute: is an ancient Irish goddess of east County Clare
had a human father and a sunbeam mother
Old Irish word meaning a youth of arms-bearing age or a servant or messenger
originally used with an epithet to name servants, as in Gilla Decair
from the tenth century on used as the first element in masculine proper names such as Gilla Cóemáin and Gilla Crist
her name follows the gilla plus gréine pattern, naming the goddess as servant or daughter of the sun

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Gillagréine is an ancient Irish goddess of east County Clare, though she remains little known. Her name survives across the region. She learned that her father was human while her mother was a sunbeam. In despair she leaped into the water of Lough Gréine, also called Lough Graney. Her body drifted to Daire Gréine and then came to rest at Tuam Gréine, the sun's tomb. She may have been an early sun goddess. MacKillop does not enter her as a deity. He enters the underlying Old Irish word gilla, which carries two senses. It can mean a young man old enough to bear weapons. It can also mean a servant or messenger, the form anglicised as gilly. At first the word took an epithet to name such servants. Gilla Decair, the Hard Servant, gives his name to Toraigheacht an Ghiolla Dheacair, the Pursuit of the Hard Gilly. After the tenth century, gilla turned into the opening element of masculine personal names. Gilla Cóemáin, a poet and chronicler who flourished between 1025 and 1075, is one example. The many-named Gilla Crist, Servant of Christ, is another. The modern reflexes are Modern Irish giolla and Scottish Gaelic gille. Gillagréine's compound name follows this same gilla plus descriptive-element pattern, with gréine meaning of the sun.

okr.objective: Document Gillagréine as a regional Irish sun goddess and explain her name through MacKillop's entry on the Old Irish word gilla.
key_results: Place Gillagréine in east County Clare and trace her path from Lough Gréine to Tuam Gréine.
Cite MacKillop's two senses of gilla as youth of arms-bearing age and as servant or messenger.
Record the use of gilla as a naming element from the tenth century onward and link it to the goddess's compound name.
